title: Mutually Exclusive Events
videoTitle: AP Statistics Topic 2.5 Mutually Exclusive Events
intro: After this lesson you can find a joint probability from a two-way table, write it with the intersection symbol, and use $P(A\cap B)$ to decide whether two events are mutually exclusive.

moments.title: Joint probability
moments.text: The probability that events $A$ and $B$ both occur. It is the probability of the intersection of $A$ and $B$.

moments.title: Intersection symbol
moments.text: $P(A\cap B)$ is read "the probability of $A$ and $B$". You may write the word "and" instead.

moments.title: Mutually exclusive (disjoint)
moments.text: Events that cannot occur at the same time. Then $P(A\cap B)=0$.

moments.title: Robotics and drama clubs
moments.text: 85 students: 30 in robotics, 45 in drama, 15 in neither. Are the clubs mutually exclusive?

moments.title: Fill a two-way table from totals
moments.text: Place the known numbers, then use row and column sums to find the missing cells.

moments.title: A single overlap is enough
moments.text: Five students are in both clubs, so the events are not mutually exclusive.

moments.title: Book or recess
moments.text: Students had to pick one option, so choosing both is impossible and the events are mutually exclusive.

moments.title: Coffee order by gender
moments.text: 150 customers: 70 male and 80 female, with hot or iced coffee.

moments.title: Not mutually exclusive pairs
moments.text: Male and iced coffee overlap in 22 customers. Female and hot coffee overlap in 28.

moments.title: Naming mutually exclusive events
moments.text: Grades 9 and 12, or two different favorite sports, cannot both happen to the same student.

moments.title: Football and 11th grade
moments.text: 23 of 200 students are both, so the joint probability is $23/200=0.115$.

cards.name: Mutually exclusive
cards.text: No outcome is in both events, so $P(A\cap B)=0$.

cards.name: Not mutually exclusive
cards.text: At least one outcome is in both events, so $P(A\cap B)>0$.

cells: Robotics club and drama club (85 students)
Choosing the book and choosing recess (pick one)

notes.label: Wording check.
notes.text: Mutually exclusive events cannot happen together. This is different from independent events, which topic 2.7 covers. Do not use the two words as if they mean the same thing.

questions.obj: Decide from a two-way table whether two clubs overlap
questions.q: A teacher has 85 students. Of these, 30 are in robotics club, 45 are in drama club, and 15 are in neither club. Are being in robotics club and being in drama club mutually exclusive?

steps.t: Put the totals and the "neither" count into a two-way table.

work.text: The row total for robotics is 30, the column total for drama is 45, the "neither" cell is 15, and the table total is 85.

steps.t: Find how many students are in at least one club.

work.text: Everyone who is not in the "neither" cell is in robotics, drama, or both.

steps.t: Find the overlap by adding the two clubs and subtracting the students in at least one.

work.text: Adding the two club totals counts the students in both clubs twice. The extra count is the overlap.
The joint probability divides the "both" cell by the table total.

steps.t: Decide: the events are mutually exclusive only if the joint probability is 0.

work.text: Five students are in both clubs, so the events can occur at the same time.

questions.answer: Robotics club and drama club are not mutually exclusive. Five of the 85 students are in both clubs, so $P(R\cap D)$ is not 0.

questions.obj: Decide when students could pick only one option
questions.q: 60 students each chose to read a book or go to recess, but could not do both. 43 chose recess and 17 chose the book. Are choosing the book and choosing recess mutually exclusive?

steps.t: Put the totals into a two-way table.

work.text: The recess total is 43, the book total is 17, and the table total is 60.

steps.t: Use the rule of the situation to fill the "both" cell.

work.text: Each student could choose only one option, so no student is in both cells.
The joint probability divides the "both" cell by the table total.

steps.t: Decide: the events are mutually exclusive only if the joint probability is 0.

work.text: The joint probability is 0, so the events cannot occur at the same time.

questions.answer: Choosing the book and choosing recess are mutually exclusive. No student chose both, so $P(\text{book}\cap\text{recess})=0$.

questions.obj: Find a joint probability and test a pair of events
questions.q: 150 customers ordered coffee: 70 were male and 80 were female. 22 of the males ordered iced coffee, and 28 of the females ordered hot coffee. Find the probability that a randomly selected customer is female and ordered hot coffee. Are being female and ordering hot coffee mutually exclusive?

steps.t: Find the cell where both events occur.

work.text: The cell for female and hot coffee is given: 28 customers.
A joint probability uses all 150 customers as the denominator.

steps.t: Decide: the events are mutually exclusive only if the joint probability is 0.

work.text: Twenty-eight customers are both female and ordered hot coffee, so the events can happen together.

steps.t: Name a pair of mutually exclusive events to check your understanding.

work.text: Male and female cannot both be true of one customer, so those events are mutually exclusive.

questions.answer: The probability that a customer is female and ordered hot coffee is about 0.187. Being female and ordering hot coffee are not mutually exclusive, because 28 customers are both.

traps.title: Justify with the joint probability
traps.weak: The clubs are not mutually exclusive.
traps.better: There are 5 students in both clubs, so $P(R\cap D)=5/85\neq0$. The events can occur at the same time, so they are not mutually exclusive.

traps.title: Adding the clubs and ignoring the overlap
traps.better: Five students are in both clubs, so 75 counts them twice. Only 70 students are in at least one club.

traps.title: Confusing mutually exclusive with independent
traps.weak: The events have nothing to do with each other, so they are mutually exclusive.
traps.better: Mutually exclusive means the events cannot occur together, so $P(A\cap B)=0$. Independence is a different idea.

traps.title: Joint probability using the wrong denominator
traps.better: A joint probability divides by the table total: $28/150\approx0.187$. Dividing by 80 gives a conditional proportion.

traps.title: Giving a pair that overlaps
traps.weak: Male and iced coffee are mutually exclusive events.
traps.better: Male and iced coffee overlap in 22 customers. Two mutually exclusive events are male and female.

questions.stem: Of 120 students, 48 are in choir, 36 are in band and 12 are in both. What is $P(\text{choir}\cap\text{band})$?
why: Correct. The joint probability divides the "both" count by the total of 120.
This divides by the choir total, so it is a conditional proportion.
This adds the two clubs without removing the overlap.
Zero would mean no student is in both clubs.

questions.stem: Which pair of events is mutually exclusive when one card is drawn from a standard deck?
opts: A red card and a queen
A face card and a spade
why: The king of hearts is both.
The queen of hearts is both.
Correct. No card is both a club and a diamond.
The king of spades is both.

questions.stem: Events $A$ and $B$ satisfy $P(A\cap B)=0.08$. Which conclusion is correct?
why: The joint probability alone does not decide independence.
Complements have a joint probability of 0.
Mutually exclusive events have a joint probability of 0.
Correct. A positive joint probability means they can occur together.

questions.stem: In a class of 30 students, 18 take French, 14 take Spanish and 6 take neither. How many take both?
why: If 2 took both, only $18+14-2=30$ students would take a language, but 6 take neither.
Correct. 24 students take a language, so both is $18+14-24=8$.
14 is the number taking Spanish, not the overlap.
Zero would mean the languages are mutually exclusive, but then $18+14=32$ would exceed 24.

sections.title: Free-response practice
sections.prompt: A school has 120 students. Of these, 48 play an instrument, 36 play a sport and 12 do both. The rest do neither.
parts: (c) Are playing an instrument and playing a sport mutually exclusive? Justify.
(d) Give one pair of mutually exclusive events from this school.
sample: (a) Instrument and sport: 12. Instrument only: 36. Sport only: 24. Neither: 48. Totals: instrument 48, sport 36, grand total 120.
(c) No. Twelve students do both, so $P(\text{instrument}\cap\text{sport})\neq0$ and the events can occur together.
(d) For example, a student in Grade 9 and a student in Grade 12 (nobody is in both grades), or "plays a sport" and "plays no sport".
